newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi army says it kills 30 rebels.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army says it kills 30 rebels.

text.p: Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army said on Monday it killed around 30 Hutu rebels in fighting south of the capital, while nine civilians were killed in a land mine explosion.
"About 30 rebels were killed by the army in Kabezi (commune, rural Bujumbura province) on Saturday. It was part of a military sweep," said army spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi.

"At 11 a.m. (0900 GMT) this morning a minibus struck an anti-tank mine in Nyamitanja (Cibitoke province). Nine civilians were killed, nine were wounded. There were 21 people in the bus and three of them escaped unhurt," Nibizi said.
More than 150,000 people have died in massacres and civil war between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels since the assassination of Burundi's first Hutu president in October 1993.
Four civilians were killed on Sunday when a minibus travelling south from the capital on National Route Three towards Rumonge hit an anti-tank mine, Nibizi said.

Nibizi blamed rebels of the main Hutu rebel National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD) for planting the mine and said about 15 civilians were aboard the bus. He had no information on any wounded.
Nibizi said the mine exploded 40 km (25 miles) south of Bujumbura in Nyaruhongoka village.
Bujumbura residents said on Monday sporadic gunfire and mortar bomb explosions were audible in the capital over the weekend but the army said there were no casualties in clashes with rebels.
A Defence Ministry official said troops were involved in an operation in the area around Bujumbura against rebels moving from the northern province of Bubanza to the south of Burundi.
The CNDD, led by former interior minister Leonard Nyangoma, on Sunday condemned the execution of six people in Bujumbura and said it might pull out of peace talks scheduled for August 25.
The CNDD said the hangings of the six in Bujumbura's central prison on Thursday violated an agreement signed in Rome in March with the Burundi government on future peace negotiations.

The accord called for creation of an international crime tribunal to judge acts of genocide and other political crimes committed in Burundi, a former Belgian colony. The United Nations last month rejected an international tribunal.
The trials of the six men, accused of participation in massacres in 1993, were conducted by local judicial authorities.
